newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia offers more autonomy to rebel territory.
newsitem.headline: Georgia offers more autonomy to rebel territory.

text.p: President Eduard Shevardnadze offered increased autonomy on Tuesday to Georgia's breakaway region of Abkhazia but ruled out any deal with the Black Sea province as broad as that between Russia and its Chechen rebels.

"We are ready to instantly resume talks on all levels, including a bilateral Georgia-Abkhazia dialogue," Shevardnadze told parliament in an annual state of the nation speech laying out a set of new proposals on the troubled issue.
Shevardnadze said Tbilisi was ready to offer Abkhazia -- which Georgia lost in a bitter separatist war in 1992-1993 -- the "widest autonomy within the framework of a single state".
The former Soviet foreign minister added that the Georgian government wanted prompt repatriation of hundreds of thousands of ethnic Georgians who fled Abkhazia during the war.
Peace in Abkhazia is vital for Georgia, which is desperate for foreign investment to kick-start an economy weakened by years of post-Soviet turmoil.
But Shevardnadze's room for manoeuvre in the lush, sub-tropical territory, a resort favoured by the Communist elite in Soviet times, is limited by Georgia's nationalist lobby.
In offering autonomy for the region, he ruled out any deal between Tbilisi and Abkhazia as equal parties.
"The option offered lately by (separatist leader Vladislav) Ardzinba is unacceptable," Shevardnadze said. "He is offering a model of the accord between Russia and Chechnya."

Russia and its rebel region of Chechnya signed a peace treaty earlier this month to end months of bloody war. The deal did not say whether Chechnya should become independent or remain part of Russia, leaving a large question mark over the accord.
Shevardnadze also said he was unhappy with the way Russia was performing its peacekeeping role in Abkhazia and reiterated that Tbilisi was reviewing Moscow's mandate.
Russian paratroopers have kept Georgia's warring sides apart since 1994, deployed along a security zone between Abkhazia and the rest of Georgia.
Georgia wants the peacekeepers to patrol more actively along a wide strip of territory along the Georgia-Abkhazia border and to help in the repatriation of refugees.
Russia's mandate was changed to meet Georgia's demands at a summit of former Soviet states earlier this year.
But Shevardnadze has since complained that Moscow has done nothing to carry out the summit's resolution.
"If in the remaining two months the summit decision is not carried out, the further presence of the peacekeeping contingent will become impossible," he said, restating his position.
Abkhaz separatists accuse Tbilisi of wanting to remove the Russian peacekeepers so it can retake the region by force.

"The Georgian side is trying to prepare its public for a new war against Abkhazia," rebel interior minister Almazbei Kchach told Reuters by telephone from the Abkhaz capital, Sukhumi. "If the peacekeepers are withdrawn, war will become inevitable."
Shevardnadze said he did not believe a new war was possible.
"The Abkhaz do not want war, which would be suicidal for them," Shevardnadze said. "We do not want war either because we have had enough of death and destruction."
